section_title: Why is the meeting tent outside the camp?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it at a distance outside the camp. He called it the Tent of Meeting, and anyone inquiring of the LORD would go to the Tent of Meeting outside the camp. 8 Then, whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would stand at the entrances to their own tents and watch Moses until he entered the tent. 9 As Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would come down and remain at the entrance, and the LORD would speak with Moses. 10 When all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance to the tent, they would stand up and worship, each one at the entrance to his own tent.
11 Thus the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Then Moses would return to the camp, but his young assistant Joshua son of Nun would not leave the tent.

context_lines: Moses pitches the meeting tent at a distance outside the camp. After the calf, that distance makes the broken relationship visible, yet it also leaves a place where people can seek the LORD. In the book’s narrative, the account of constructing the tabernacle still lies ahead; here the emphasis is on meeting God and hearing Him.

The people watch Moses go out, see the cloud at the entrance, and worship from their own tent doors. God continues speaking with Moses, and Joshua remains at the tent when Moses returns to the camp. The passage does not condemn the people’s worship or explain their private motives.

God speaks with Moses as a person speaks with a friend. This describes direct, familiar communication. Later in this same chapter, God tells Moses that he cannot see His face and live. Those two statements need to be read together: close conversation is not the same thing as an unrestricted sight of God’s glory. [Numbers 12:5–8](https://biblehub.com/bsb/numbers/12.htm) likewise contrasts the clarity of God’s communication with Moses with the dreams and riddles given to other prophets.
common_interpretation_lines: Readers differ over which tent this is. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) treats it as a meeting place used before the later tabernacle; [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/exodus/33.htm) considers Moses’ own tent or another earlier place of worship. [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/exodus/33.htm) rejects the private-tent explanation and identifies it as God’s sacred sanctuary, reading the arrangement of these events differently. All three see its distance from the camp as a sign of separation after the calf.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-moses-called-exodus/) emphasizes the friendship and kindness in God’s speech to Moses; [Calvin](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/exodus/33.htm) also distinguishes such close revelation from seeing God in His fullness. The phrase about speaking face to face need not be turned into a contradiction with verse 20.
god_plan_lines: God’s clear communication with Moses serves the people, not Moses alone. [Numbers 12:5–8](https://biblehub.com/bsb/numbers/12.htm) describes him as faithful in God’s house. [Hebrews 3:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/3.htm) takes up that description and points beyond him: Moses serves within God’s household, while Christ is the Son over it. His faithful service belongs to a larger story whose center is Jesus.

The New Testament also describes a greater nearness for God’s people together. Through Christ, Jews and Gentiles have access to the Father by one Spirit and are being built into a dwelling for God ([Ephesians 2:13–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/2.htm)). This does not make every detail of the outside tent a prediction. It shows the wider direction of God’s work: bringing His people near to Himself.
